senses: advocate, attendant (friend who supports in a trial)
la:noun:advocatus.html:
advŏcātus, i, m.,
a legal assistant, counsellor, etc., v. advoco fin.

senses: to run, dash or come to or toward, swoop on
la:verb:advolo.html:
ad-vŏlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n.,
to fly to or toward; constr. with ad, in, dat., or acc., Rudd. II. p. 136.
Lit., of birds: avis advolans ad eas avīs,: in agrum Volaterranum palumbium vise mari advolat,: papilio luminibus lucernarum advolans, .—
Metaph., of other things, to fly to, run to, come to (class.): vox mihi advolavit ad aurīs,; so ; : imago ad nos, * : ad urbem,: in Formianum,: Larino Romam,: ejus (Britanniae) εἴδωλον mihi advolabit ad pectus, : hostes ex omnibus partibus ad pabulatores,: classem advolaturam esse,: in auxilium,: fama advolat Aeneae,; Manil. ap. P.—With acc.: rostra Cato advolat,; .

senses: to turn the mind to, give attention or draw attention to, attend
la:verb:adverto.html:
ad-verto (archaic advor-), ti, sum, 3, v. a.,
to turn a thing to or toward a place (in this signif., without animus; mostly poet.; syn.: observare, animadvertere, videre, cognoscere).
Lit.
In gen., with in or dat.: illa sese huc advorterat in hanc nostram plateam,: in quamcunque domus lumina partem,; cf. : malis numen,: huc aures, huc, quaeso, advertite sensus,; cf. .—
Esp., a naut. t. t., to turn, direct, steer a ship to a place: classem in portum, Drak.: terrae proras,; : Colchos puppim,.—Absol.: profugi advertere coloni,landed,; hence also transf. to other things: aequore cursum,: pedem ripae,: urbi agmen,: adverti with acc.poet. for verti ad: Scythicas advertitur oras, (cf. adducor litora remis, , and Rudd. II. p. 327).
Fig.
Animum (in the poets and Livy also animos, rarely mentem) advertere; absol., or with adv. or ad aliquid, or alicui rei, to direct the mind, thoughts, or attention to a thing, to advert to, give attention to, attend to, to heed, observe, remark: si voles advortere animum, Enn. ap. Var. L. L. 7, § 89 Müll. (Trag. v. 386 Vahl.): facete advortis animum tuum ad animum meum,: nunc huc animum advortite ambo,: advertunt animos ad religionem,: monitis animos advertite nostris,: animum etiam levissimis rebus adverterent,.—With ne, when the object of attention is expressed: ut animum advertant, ne quos offendant,: adverterent animos, ne quid novi tumultūs oriretur,.—
Animum advertere, to observe a thing by directing the mind to it, to observe, to notice, to remark, to perceive (in the class. period contracted to animadvertere, q. v.).—Constr. with two accusatives, animum advertere aliquid (where aliquid may be regarded as depending on the prep. in comp., Roby, § 1118, or on animum advertere, considered as one idea, to observe), with acc. and inf., or rel. clause (the first mode of construction, most frequent with the pronouns id, hoc, illud, etc., is for the most part ante-class., and appears in Caes., Cic., and Sall. as an archaism): et hoc animum advorte,: hanc edictionem,: haec animum te advertere par est,: animum adverti columellam e dumis eminentem,; : Postquam id animum advertit,; : quidam Ligus animum advortit inter saxa repentīs cocleas,. In Vitruv. once with hinc: ut etiam possumus hinc animum advertere,as we can hence perceive,.—With the acc. and inf.: postquam tantopere id vos velle animum advorteram,: animum advertit magnas esse copiashostium instructas,: cum animum adverteret locum relictum esse, Auct. B. Alex. 31; .—With the rel. clause: nunc quam rem vitio dent, quaeso, animum advortite, : quid ille sperare possit, animum adverte, Dolab. ap. : quam multarum rerum ipse ignarus esset ... animum advertit,. Sometimes advertere alone = animum advertere; so once in Cicero's letters: nam advertebatur Pompeii familiares assentiri Volcatio, Fam. 1, 1 (although here, as well as almost everywhere, the readings fluctuate between advertere and animadvertere; cf. Orell. ad h. l.; animadvertebatur, B. and K.). So Verg. in the imp.: qua ratione quod instat, Confieri possit, paucis, adverte, docebo,attend!.—In the histt., esp. Tac. and Pliny, more frequently: donec advertit Tiberius,: Zenobiam advertere pastores,: advertere quosdam cultu externo in sedibus senatorum,: quotiens novum aliquid adverterat, al.: hirudo quam sanguisugam appellari adverto,: ut multos adverto credidisse,. Still more rarely, advertere animo: animis advertite vestris,: hanc scientiam ad nostros pervenisse animo adverto,; cf. Drak. ad .—
To draw or turn something, esp. the attention of another, to or upon one's self (in the histt.): gemitus ac planctus militum aures oraque advertere,: octo aquilae imperatorem advertere,: recentia veteraque odia advertit, drew them on himself, al.—
To call the attention of one to a definite act, i. e. to admonish of it, to urge to it (cf. II. A.): non docet admonitio, sed advertit,i. e. directs attention,: advertit ea res Vespasiani animum, ut, etc.,.—
Advertere in aliquem, for the more usual animadvertere in aliquem, to attend to one, i. e. to punish one (only in Tac.): in P. Marcium consules more prisco advertere,: ut in reliquos Sejani liberos adverteretur, (cf. : animadvertere).—Hence,
adversus (archaic advor-), a, um, P. a., turned to or toward a thing, with the face or front toward, standing over against, opposite, before, in front of (opp. aversus).
In gen.: solem adversum intueri,: Iris ... Mille trahens varios adverso sole colores,; : antipodes adversis vestigiis stant contra nostra vestigia,: dentes adversi acuti (the sharp front teeth) morsu dividunt escas, : quod is collis, tantum adversus in latitudinem patebat, quantum etc., Herz. So, hostes adversi, who make front against one advancing or retreating, : L. Cotta legatus in adversum os fundā vulneratur,in front,; cf. ; al.; hence, vulnus adversum, a wound in front (on the contr., vulnus aversum, a wound in the back), : adversis vulneribus,: judicibus cicatrices adversas ostendere,: cicatrices populus Romanus aspiceret adverso corpore exceptas,: impetus hostium adversos, Auct. B. Alex. 8: Romani advorso colle evadunt,ascend the hill in front,: adversa signa,: legiones quas Visellius et C. Silius adversis itineribus objecerant,i. e. marches in which they went to meet the enemy,: sed adverso fulgure (by a flash of lightning falling directly before him) pavefactus est Nero, : armenta egit Hannibal in adversos montes,; cf. ; so ; : qui timet his adversa,the opposite of this,—Hence, of rivers: flumine adverso, up the stream, against the stream: in adversum flumen contendere,: adverso feruntur flumine,; so : adverso amne,; adverso Tiberi subvehi, (opp. to secundā aquā, down stream, with the stream: rate in secundam aquam labente,); and of winds, opposed to a vessel's course, head winds, contrary winds, consequently unfavorable, adverse: navigationes adversis ventis praecluduntur, Auct. B. Alex. 8: adversissimi navigantibus venti,.—Subst.: adversum, i, the opposite: hic ventus a septentrionibus oriens adversum tenet Athenis proficiscentibus,

holds the opposite to those sailing from Athens, i. e. blows against them, (so Nipperdey; but v. Hand, Turs. I. p. 183). —Adv.: ex adverso, also written exadverso and exadversum, opposite to, over against, ἐκ τοῦ ἐναντίου: portus ex adverso urbi positus,.—With gen.: Patrae ex adverso Aetoliae et fluminis Eveni,.—Without case: cum ex adverso starent classes,; so ; .—In adversum, to the opposite side, against: et duo in adversum immissi per moenia currus,against each other,; so ; cf. ; in adversum Romani subiere,; .—

In hostile opposition to, adverse to, unfavorable, unpropitious (opp. secundus; frequent and class.): conqueri fortunam adversam, Pac. ap. : hic dies pervorsus atque advorsus mihi obtigit,: advorsus nemini,: mentes improborum mihi infensae et adversae,: acclamatio,: adversā avi aliquid facere, vet. poët. ap. : adversis auspiciis,: adversum omen,: adversissima auspicia,: adversae res, misfortune, calamity, adverse fortune: ut adversas res, sic secundas immoderate ferre levitatis est,; cf.: adversi casus,: adversae rerum undae,a sea of troubles,: omnia secundissima nobis, adversissima illis accidisse, Caes. ap. (the sup. is found also in Cæs. B. C. 3, 107): quae magistratus ille dicet, secundis auribus, quae ab nostrum quo dicentur, adversis accipietis?: adversus annus frugibus,: valetudo adversa,i. e. sickness,: adversum proelium,an unsuccessful engagement,; cf. 8, 31: adverso rumore esse,to be in bad repute, to have a bad reputation,: adversa subsellia,on which the opposition sit,.—Sometimes met. of feeling, contrary to, hated, hateful, odious: quīs omnia regna advorsa sint,; cf. Bentl.—Comp.: neque est aliud adversius,.—* Adv.: adver-sē, self-contradictorily, .—ad-versum, i, subst., esp. in the plur. adversa, misfortune, calamity, disaster, adversity, evil, mischief: advorsa ejus per te tecta sient,: nihil adversi,: si quid adversi accidisset,; cf. ; : secunda felices, adversa magnos probant,; esp. freq. in Tac.: prospera et adversa pop. Rom., Ann. 1, 1: adversa tempestatum et fluctuum,; so ; ; ; 4, 13 al.—Subst.: adversus, i, m., an opponent, adversary (rare): multosque mortalīs ea causa advorsos habeo,.—In Quint. also once ad-versa, ae, f., subst., a female opponent or adversary: natura noverca fuerit, si facultatem dicendi sociam scelerum, adversam innocentiae, invenit, 12, 1, 2.—
In rhet., opposed to another of the same genus, e. g. sapientia and stultitia: Haec quae ex eodem genere contraria sunt, appellantur adversa, .

la:prep:adversus.html:
adversus (archaic advor-), a, um,

la:noun:adventus.html:
adventus, ūs (
gen. adventi, ; cf. P.), m.
advenio
, a coming, an approach, arrival (class., also in plur.).
Lit.: Beluarum [haec] ferarum adventus ne taetret loca, Pac. ap. (Trag. Rel. p. 114 Rib.): adventum Veneris fugiunt venti,: in adventu Titi,: ad urbem,: in urbes,: ut me levārat tuus adventus, sic discessus afflixit,: praestolabor adventum tuum,: adventibus se offerre, i. e. advenientibus obviam ire,: lucis,: consulis Romam,—Sometimes of the approach of an enemy: nisi adventus ejus appropinquāsset,; so ; .—
Transf., the state of having arrived, an arrival, the being present by arriving (cf. advenio, B.): quorum adventu altera castra ad alteram oppidi partem ponit,: horum adventu tanta rerum commutatio est facta,.—
Fig.: adventus in animos et introitus imaginum,: malorum,: exspectantes adventum gloriae Dei,: nuptiarum,.

la:verb:advenio.html:
ad-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4, v. a.,
to come to a place, to reach, arrive at (syn.: accedere, adventare, adire, appellere, adesse); constr. absol., with ad, in, or acc.
Lit.: verum praetor advenit, Naev. ap. (Bell. Pun. v. 44 Vahl.): ad vos adveniens, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 14 Vahl.): ad forum,; so ; ; cf. : advenis modo? Admodum,; Caecil. ap. : procul a patria domoque,: ad auris,; so ; ; : in montem Oetam, Att. ap. : in provinciam, (so : somnus in ignotos oculos): ex Hyperboreis Delphos,: est quiddam, advenientem non esse peregrinum atque hospitem,; ; .—With simple acc.: Tyriam urbem,: unde hos advenias labores, (whether in , properantibus Blaesus advenit, the first word is a dat., as Rudd. II. p. 135, supposes, or an abl. absol., may still be doubted).—Also with sup.: tentatum advenis,; so .—
Transf.
Poet., in adding an entire thought as an amplification of what precedes (for accedo, q. v.): praeter enim quam quod morbis cum corporis aegret, Advenit id quod eam de rebus saepe futuris Macerat, etc., beside that it often suffers with the body itself, this often occurs, that it is itself tormented in regard to the future, etc., .—
In the perf., the act of coming being considered as completed, to have come, i. e. to be somewhere, to be present (v. adventus, B.; cf. Herz. ad ); of time: mterea dies advenit, quo die, etc.,appeared,; so, ubi dies advenit,: advenit proficiscendi hora,: tempus meum nondum advenit,.—
To come into one's possession, to accrue, ; cf. —
To come by conveyance, to be brought; of a letter: advenere litterae (for allatae sunt),.

la:verb:advoco.gloss: to call, invite or summon someone to a place, invoke
senses: to call, invite or summon someone to a place, invoke
to call in as aid, assistant, witness or counsellor
la:verb:advoco.html:
ad-vŏco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to call or summon one to a place, esp. for counsel, aid, etc.; constr. absol., with ad, in, or dat.
In gen.
Lit.: ego Tiresiam advocabo et consulam quid faciendum censeat,: contionem,: aliquem ad obsignandum,; so : viros primarios in consilium,; so : ego vos, quo pauca monerem, advocavi,: eo (i. e. in aedem Concordiae) senatum advocat,: (Deus) advocabit caelum desursum,: advocari gaudiis,to be invited,: aegro,: causis,.—
Trop.: animum ad se ipsum advocamus,we turn the mind upon itself, call the thoughts home,: non desiderat fortitudo advocatam iracundiam,; so ; . —
Esp.
In judicial lang., t. t., to avail one's self of some one in a cause, as aid, assistant, witness, counsellor, etc., to call in: aliquem alicui,; so ; : aliquot mihi Amicos advocabo,: viros bonos complures advocat,: in his, quos tibi advocasti, al.—Also used of the friend of the plaintiff or defendant, who calls in his friends to aid in the suit: Oppianicus in judicio Scamandri aderat, frequens advocabat,.—Hence, transf. to other things, to call to one's aid, to call to for help, to summon: desuper Alcides telis premit omniaque arma Advocat,: secretas artes,: ad conamina noctem,; : aliquid in tutelam securitatis suae,: vires suas,.—
To get a respite, to delay, ; v. advocatio, II. C. —
To give consolation, to console (in imitation of the Gr. παρακαλεῖν), .!*? In the phrase ADVOCAPIT CONCTOS, in the song of the Fratres Arvales, Grotef. (Gr. II. 290) explains advocapit as an old imperat., instead of advocabite.Hence, advŏcātus, i, m.
In the class. per., in judicial lang., one who is called by one of the parties in a suit to aid as a witness or counsel, a legal assistant, counsellor (diff. from patronus or orator, who spoke for a client engaged in a suit; from cognitor, who appeared in the name of such parties as had themselves been at first in court; and from procurator, who appeared for such as were absent,; Ruhnk. ad ; Heind. ad ; v. Smith's Dict. Antiq.): quaeso, ut advocatus mihi adsis neve abeas,; so ; ; ; ; : adversusne illum causam dicerem, cui veneram advocatus?; so ; ; : quis eum umquam non modo in patroni, sed in laudatoris aut advocati loco viderat,; : venire advocatum alicui in rem praesentem,, etc.; .—
In the post-Aug. per., for patronus, orator, etc., who conducted a process for any one, an advocate, attorney, etc., ; cf. ; fin.; 9, 3, 22; ; ; and 33.—
Esp., in eccl. Lat., of Christ as our intercessor, advocate: advocatum habemus apud Patrem, Jesum Christum,.—
Transf., in gen., an assistant, helper, friend: se in fugam conferunt unā amici advocatique ejus,.

la:adj:adversarius.html:
adversārĭus, a, um, adj.
adversus
.
Turned toward one or lying before one's eyes; hence, adversārĭa, ōrum (sc. scripta), in mercantile language, a book at hand in which all matters are entered temporarily as they occur, a waste-book, day-book, journal, memoranda, etc.: Quid est quod neglegenter scribamus adversaria? quid est. quod diligenter conficiamus tabulas? Qua de causa? Quia haec sunt menstrua, illae sunt aeternae: haec delentur statim, illae servantur sancte, etc., and 7.
Standing opposite or opposed to one, as an antagonist, in any kind of contest, in which the contending parties may be the best friends, e. g. in elections, auctions, discussions, etc. (cf. Doed. Syn. 4, 395; in gen., only of persons, while contrarius is used of things, P.).
Adj.: tribunus seditiosis adversarius,,

94: vis juri adversaria,: opinio oratori,: duces,: populus, adversarius, invidus etiam potentiae,in hostile opposition to those in power,: factio,: frater,—

Subst.: adversārĭus, i, m., an antagonist, opponent, adversary, an enemy, rival (the most usual class. signif. of the word): valentiorem nactus adversarium,: injuria adversariūm, prol. alt. 14; cf. : tribuni plebis illius adversarii, defensores mei,; so ; ; ; ; .—Of wrestlers and other athletæ: pugiles etiam cum feriunt adversarium ... ingemiscunt,; also, in auctions, of opposing bidders: res major est quam facultates nostrae praesertim adversario et cupido et locuplete,; cf. .—In Cic. also in the fem.: adversārĭa, ae: est tibi gravis adversaria constituta et parata, incredibilis quaedam exspectatio,; and in the neutr. plur.: adversārĭa, ōrum, the arguments, assertions of the antagonist, .!*? The histt. more freq. than Cic. and Hor. use adversarius like hostis for an enemy in war: adversarios in fuga esse,: multitudo adversariorum,: montem occupat, ne forte cedentibus adversariis receptui foret,; ; ; ; ; ; ; cf. advosem in Müll.

la:verb:advento.gloss: to come continually nearer to a point, approach, arrive at, press forward, march on, come to, draw near
senses: to come continually nearer to a point, approach, arrive at, press forward, march on, come to, draw near
la:verb:advento.html:
advento, āvi, ātum, 1,
v. freq. [id.], to come continually nearer to a point (cotidianis itineribus accedere et appropinquare, Manut. ad ), to come on, to approach, to arrive at or come to (esp. with the access. idea of speed, haste; only a few times in Cic., and never in his orations; in the histt. used esp. of the advance of the enemy's army in military order, and the like, cf. Herz. ad Auct. B. G. 8, 20; hence without the signif. of a hostile attack, which adoriri and aggredi have); constr. absol., with adv., prepp., the dat., or acc., cf. Rudd. II. p. 136.
Absol.: multi alii adventant, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 73 Vahl.): te id admonitum advento,: quod jam tempus adventat,advances with rapid strides,: adventans senectus,: tu adventare ac prope adesse jam debes,. 17: Caesar adventare, jam jamque adesse ejus equites falso nuntiabantur,; Auct. B. G. 8, 20.—
With adv. of place: quo cum adventaret, etc., Auct. B. G. 8, 26.—
With prepp.: ad Italiam,: ad urbem,: sub ipsam finem,: in subsidium, .—
With dat.: adventante fatali urbi clade,: accipiendo Armeniae regno adventabat,: portis,.—(ε) With acc. (cf. advenio): propinqua Seleuciae adventabat,: barbaricos pagos ad ventans,; so of name of town: postquam Romam adventabant,.

la:verb:adveho.html:
ad-vĕho, xi, ctum, 3, v. a. (advexti = advexisti, ;
advexe = advexisse,), to conduct, carry, convey, bear, bring, etc., a person or thing to a place; and pass., to be carried, to ride, to come to a place upon a horse, in a carriage, ship, etc. (syn.: invehere, inferre, deferre; class., and in the histt. very freq.): eam huc mulierem in Ephesum advehit,; ; so ; : istam nunc times, quae advectast,: ex agris frumentum Romam,: ad urbem advectus,: sacerdos advecta (curru) in fanum,: equo advectus ad fluminis ripam,: sestertiūm sexagies, quod advexerat Domitius,: vasa aerea advexerunt populi,: Marius Uticam advehitur,: in eam partem citato equo advectus,: quae (naves) advexerant legatos,; —So ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; —Also: humero advehit,.—In Verg. and Tac. also with acc. pers.: advehitur Teucros,: equo collustrans omnia ut quosque advectus erat, etc.,; so .

verb. freq. [adverto], to turn to a thing: animum advorsavi sedulo, ne, etc.,.

la:verb:adversor.gloss: to stand opposite; to be against, resist, oppose; withstand
senses: to stand opposite; to be against, resist, oppose; withstand
la:verb:adversor.html:
adversor (archaic advor-), ātus, 1, v. dep.
adversus
: alicui,
to stand opposite to one, to be against, i. e. to resist or oppose (in his opinions, feelings, intentions, etc.; while resistere and obsistere denote resistance through external action, Doed. Syn. 4, 303; cf. adversarius; class.; freq. in Cic.); constr. with dat. or absol.: idem ego arbitror nee tibi advorsari certum est de istac re usquam, soror,, 21: meis praeceptis,; so : mihi,; : hujus libidini,: ornamentis tuis,: Isocrati,: commodis,: adversantes imperio Domini,: invitā Minervā, id est, adversante et repugnante natura,: non adversatur jus, quo minus, etc.,: adversante vento,: adversantibus amicis,: adversans factio,: adversantibus diis,: non adversata petenti Annuit,; al.!*?
In Tac. constr. also adversari aliquem, H. 1, 1; 1, 38.—
In Plaut. pleonastic, adversari contra, Cas. 2, 3, 35, and adversari adversus aliquid, Mer. 2, 3, 43.

la:adj:advena.html:
advĕna, ae (acc. to Valer. Prob. 1439 and 1445 P., m., f., and n., like verna; cf.
, however, P.: Inveniuntur quaedam ex communibus etiam neutri generi adjuncta, sed figurate per ἀλλοιότητα, ut advena, mancipium) [advenio], one who comes to a place; a foreigner, stranger, or alien; and adj., strange, foreign, alien, etc. (syn.: peregrinus, externus, exterus, alienus, alienigena; opp. indigena, native; class. both in prose and poetry).
Lit.: defessus perrogitandod advenas Fuit de gnatis, Pac. ap. P. (Trag. Rel. p. 116 Rib.): advena anus paupercula, * : volucres,: advenam gruem,: illas (ciconias) hiemis, has (grues) aestatis advenas,: Zeno Citieus advena,: advena possessor agelli,: exercitus advena,; : Tibris advena,as flowing from Etruria into the Roman territory,: amor advena,love for a foreign maiden,: advenae reges,; : advenae Romani,.—
Fig., a stranger to a thing, i.e. ignorant, unskilled, inexperienced = ignarus: ne in nostra patria peregrini atque advenae esse videamur,; cf.: non hospites, sed peregrini atque advenae nominabamur,; hence, poet. with gen.: belli,.

la:noun:advena.html:
advĕna, ae (acc. to Valer. Prob. 1439 and 1445 P., m., f., and n., like verna; cf.
, however, P.: Inveniuntur quaedam ex communibus etiam neutri generi adjuncta, sed figurate per ἀλλοιότητα, ut advena, mancipium) [advenio], one who comes to a place; a foreigner, stranger, or alien; and adj., strange, foreign, alien, etc. (syn.: peregrinus, externus, exterus, alienus, alienigena; opp. indigena, native; class. both in prose and poetry).
Lit.: defessus perrogitandod advenas Fuit de gnatis, Pac. ap. P. (Trag. la:verb:advenio#2.html:
ad-vĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4, v. a.,
to come to a place, to reach, arrive at (syn.: accedere, adventare, adire, appellere, adesse); constr. absol., with ad, in, or acc.
Lit.: verum praetor advenit, Naev. ap. (Bell. Pun. v. 44 Vahl.): ad vos adveniens, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 14 Vahl.): ad forum,; so ; ; cf. : advenis modo? Admodum,; Caecil. ap. : procul a patria domoque,: ad auris,; so ; ; : in montem Oetam, Att. ap. : in provinciam, (so : somnus in ignotos oculos): ex Hyperboreis Delphos,: est quiddam, advenientem non esse peregrinum atque hospitem,; ; .—With simple acc.: Tyriam urbem,: unde hos advenias labores, (whether in , properantibus Blaesus advenit, the first word is a dat., as Rudd. II. p. 135, supposes, or an abl. absol., may still be doubted).—Also with sup.: tentatum advenis,; so .—
Transf.
Poet., in adding an entire thought as an amplification of what precedes (for accedo, q. v.): praeter enim quam quod morbis cum corporis aegret, Advenit id quod eam de rebus saepe futuris Macerat, etc., beside that it often suffers with the body itself, this often occurs, that it is itself tormented in regard to the future, etc., .—
In the perf., the act of coming being considered as completed, to have come, i. e. to be somewhere, to be present (v. adventus, B.; cf. Herz. ad ); of time: mterea dies advenit, quo die, etc.,appeared,; so, ubi dies advenit,: advenit proficiscendi hora,: tempus meum nondum advenit,.—
To come into one's possession, to accrue, ; cf. —
To come by conveyance, to be brought; of a letter: advenere litterae (for allatae sunt),.

la:verb:adverto#2.html:
ad-verto (archaic advor-), ti, sum, 3, v. a.,
to turn a thing to or toward a place (in this signif., without animus; mostly poet.; syn.: observare, animadvertere, videre, cognoscere).
Lit.
In gen., with in or dat.: illa sese huc advorterat in hanc nostram plateam,: in quamcunque domus lumina partem,; cf. : malis numen,: huc aures, huc, quaeso, advertite sensus,; cf. .—
Esp., a naut. t. t., to turn, direct, steer a ship to a place: classem in portum, Drak.: terrae proras,; : Colchos puppim,.—Absol.: profugi advertere coloni,landed,; hence also transf. to other things: aequore cursum,: pedem ripae,: urbi agmen,: adverti with acc.poet. for verti ad: Scythicas advertitur oras, (cf. adducor litora remis, , and Rudd. II. p. 327).
Fig.
Animum (in the poets and Livy also animos, rarely mentem) advertere; absol., or with adv. or ad aliquid, or alicui rei, to direct the mind, thoughts, or attention to a thing, to advert to, give attention to, attend to, to heed, observe, remark: si voles advortere animum, Enn. ap. Var. L. L. 7, § 89 Müll. (Trag. v. 386 Vahl.): facete advortis animum tuum ad animum meum,: nunc huc animum advortite ambo,: advertunt animos ad religionem,: monitis animos advertite nostris,: animum etiam levissimis rebus adverterent,.—With ne, when the object of attention is expressed: ut animum advertant, ne quos offendant,: adverterent animos, ne quid novi tumultūs oriretur,.—
Animum advertere, to observe a thing by directing the mind to it, to observe, to notice, to remark, to perceive (in the class. period contracted to animadvertere, q. v.).—Constr. with two accusatives, animum advertere aliquid (where aliquid may be regarded as depending on the prep. in comp., Roby, § 1118, or on animum advertere, considered as one idea, to observe), with acc. and inf., or rel. clause (the first mode of construction, most frequent with the pronouns id, hoc, illud, etc., is for the most part ante-class., and appears in Caes., Cic., and Sall. as an archaism): et hoc animum advorte,: hanc edictionem,: haec animum te advertere par est,: animum adverti columellam e dumis eminentem,; : Postquam id animum advertit,; : quidam Ligus animum advortit inter saxa repentīs cocleas,. In Vitruv. once with hinc: ut etiam possumus hinc animum advertere,as we can hence perceive,.—With the acc. and inf.: postquam tantopere id vos velle animum advorteram,: animum advertit magnas esse copiashostium instructas,: cum animum adverteret locum relictum esse, Auct. B. Alex. 31; .—With the rel. clause: nunc quam rem vitio dent, quaeso, animum advortite, : quid ille sperare possit, animum adverte, Dolab. ap. : quam multarum rerum ipse ignarus esset ... animum advertit,. Sometimes advertere alone = animum advertere; so once in Cicero's letters: nam advertebatur Pompeii familiares assentiri Volcatio, Fam. 1, 1 (although here, as well as almost everywhere, the readings fluctuate between advertere and animadvertere; cf. Orell. ad h. l.; animadvertebatur, B. and K.). So Verg. in the imp.: qua ratione quod instat, Confieri possit, paucis, adverte, docebo,attend!.—In the histt., esp. Tac. and Pliny, more frequently: donec advertit Tiberius,: Zenobiam advertere pastores,: advertere quosdam cultu externo in sedibus senatorum,: quotiens novum aliquid adverterat, al.: hirudo quam sanguisugam appellari adverto,: ut multos adverto credidisse,. Still more rarely, advertere animo: animis advertite vestris,: hanc scientiam ad nostros pervenisse animo adverto,; cf. Drak. ad .—
To draw or turn something, esp. the attention of another, to or upon one's self (in the histt.): gemitus ac planctus militum aures oraque advertere,: octo aquilae imperatorem advertere,: recentia veteraque odia advertit, drew them on himself, al.—
To call the attention of one to a definite act, i. e. to admonish of it, to urge to it (cf. II. A.): non docet admonitio, sed advertit,i. e. directs attention,: advertit ea res Vespasiani animum, ut, etc.,.—
Advertere in aliquem, for the more usual animadvertere in aliquem, to attend to one, i. e. to punish one (only in Tac.): in P. Marcium consules more prisco advertere,: ut in reliquos Sejani liberos adverteretur, (cf. : animadvertere).—Hence,
adversus (archaic advor-), a, um, P. a., turned to or toward a thing, with the face or front toward, standing over against, opposite, before, in front of (opp. aversus).
In gen.: solem adversum intueri,: Iris ... Mille trahens varios adverso sole colores,; : antipodes adversis vestigiis stant contra nostra vestigia,: dentes adversi acuti (the sharp front teeth) morsu dividunt escas, : quod is collis, tantum adversus in latitudinem patebat, quantum etc., Herz. So, hostes adversi, who make front against one advancing or retreating, : L. Cotta legatus in adversum os fundā vulneratur,in front,; cf. ; al.; hence, vulnus adversum, a wound in front (on the contr., vulnus aversum, a wound in the back), : adversis vulneribus,: judicibus cicatrices adversas ostendere,: cicatrices populus Romanus aspiceret adverso corpore exceptas,: impetus hostium adversos, Auct. B. Alex. 8: Romani advorso colle evadunt,ascend the hill in front,: adversa signa,: legiones quas Visellius et C. Silius adversis itineribus objecerant,i. e. marches in which they went to meet the enemy,: sed adverso fulgure (by a flash of lightning falling directly before him) pavefactus est Nero, : armenta egit Hannibal in adversos montes,; cf. ; so ; : qui timet his adversa,the opposite of this,—Hence, of rivers: flumine adverso, up the stream, against the stream: in adversum flumen contendere,: adverso feruntur flumine,; so : adverso amne,; adverso Tiberi subvehi, (opp. to secundā aquā, down stream, with the stream: rate in secundam aquam labente,); and of winds, opposed to a vessel's course, head winds, contrary winds, consequently unfavorable, adverse: navigationes adversis ventis praecluduntur, Auct. B. Alex. 8: adversissimi navigantibus venti,.—Subst.: adversum, i, the opposite: hic ventus a septentrionibus oriens adversum tenet Athenis proficiscentibus,

holds the opposite to those sailing from Athens, i. e. blows against them, (so Nipperdey; but v. Hand, Turs. I. p. 183). —Adv.: ex adverso, also written exadverso and exadversum, opposite to, over against, ἐκ τοῦ ἐναντίου: portus ex adverso urbi positus,.—With gen.: Patrae ex adverso Aetoliae et fluminis Eveni,.—Without case: cum ex adverso starent classes,; so ; .—In adversum, to the opposite side, against: et duo in adversum immissi per moenia currus,against each other,; so ; cf. ; in adversum Romani subiere,; .—

In hostile opposition to, adverse to, unfavorable, unpropitious (opp. secundus; frequent and class.): conqueri fortunam adversam, Pac. ap. : hic dies pervorsus atque advorsus mihi obtigit,: advorsus nemini,: mentes improborum mihi infensae et adversae,: acclamatio,: adversā avi aliquid facere, vet. poët. ap. : adversis auspiciis,: adversum omen,: adversissima auspicia,: adversae res, misfortune, calamity, adverse fortune: ut adversas res, sic secundas immoderate ferre levitatis est,; cf.: adversi casus,: adversae rerum undae,a sea of troubles,: omnia secundissima nobis, adversissima illis accidisse, Caes. ap. (the sup. is found also in Cæs. B. C. 3, 107): quae magistratus ille dicet, secundis auribus, quae ab nostrum quo dicentur, adversis accipietis?: adversus annus frugibus,: valetudo adversa,i. e. sickness,: adversum proelium,an unsuccessful engagement,; cf. 8, 31: adverso rumore esse,to be in bad repute, to have a bad reputation,: adversa subsellia,on which the opposition sit,.—Sometimes met. of feeling, contrary to, hated, hateful, odious: quīs omnia regna advorsa sint,; cf. Bentl.—Comp.: neque est aliud adversius,.—* Adv.: adver-sē, self-contradictorily, .—ad-versum, i, subst., esp. in the plur. adversa, misfortune, calamity, disaster, adversity, evil, mischief: advorsa ejus per te tecta sient,: nihil adversi,: si quid adversi accidisset,; cf. ; : secunda felices, adversa magnos probant,; esp. freq. in Tac.: prospera et adversa pop. Rom., Ann. 1, 1: adversa tempestatum et fluctuum,; so ; ; ; 4, 13 al.—Subst.: adversus, i, m., an opponent, adversary (rare): multosque mortalīs ea causa advorsos habeo,.—In Quint. also once ad-versa, ae, f., subst., a female opponent or adversary: natura noverca fuerit, si facultatem dicendi sociam scelerum, adversam innocentiae, invenit, 12, 1, 2.—
In rhet., opposed to another of the same genus, e. g. sapientia and stultitia: Haec quae ex eodem genere contraria sunt, appellantur adversa, .

la:adj:adventicius.html:
adventīcĭus (not -tĭus), a, um, adj.
advenio
,
that is present by coming, coming from abroad, foreign, strange (extrinsecus ad nos perveniens non nostrum, aut nostro labore paratum, Ern. Clav. Cic.; opp. proprius, innatus, insitus, etc.; in Cic. very freq., elsewhere rare).
In gen.: genus (avium), (cf. advena): Mithridates magnis adventiciis copiis juvabatur,; so, auxilium,: externus et adventicius tepor,: externa atque adventicia visio,proceeding from the senses,: doctrina transmarina et adventicia,: dos,given by another than the father,.—
Esp.
That is added to what is customary, or happens out of course, unusual, extraordinary: fructus,; so, casus,. —
That is acquired without one's own effort: adventicia pecunia, obtained, not from one's own possessions, but by inheritance, usury, presents, etc., ; : humor adventicius,rain,: adventiciae res,.—
That pertains to arrival (adventus): adventicia cena,a banquet given on one's arrival, (cf. adventorius).—Adv. phrase: ex adventicio, from without, extrinsically: quidquid est hoc, quod circa nos ex adventicio fulget, liberi, honores, etc.,.

adversus
: alicui,
to stand opposite to one, to be against, i. e. to resist or oppose (in his opinions, feelings, intentions, etc.; while resistere and obsistere denote resistance through external action, Doed. Syn. 4, 303; cf. adversarius; class.; freq. in Cic.); constr. with dat. or absol.: idem ego arbitror nee tibi advorsari certum est de istac re usquam, soror,, 21: meis praeceptis,; so : mihi,; : hujus libidini,: ornamentis tuis,: Isocrati,: commodis,: adversantes imperio Domini,: invitā Minervā, id est, adversante et repugnante natura,: non adversatur jus, quo minus, etc.,: adversante vento,: adversantibus amicis,: adversans factio,: adversantibus diis,: non adversata petenti Annuit,; al.!*?

la:verb:advigilo.html:
ad-vĭgĭlo, āre, 1, v. n.,
to watch by or at, to keep guard over, to be watch ful, vigilant for; constr. with ad or dat., Rudd. II. p. 136
Lit.: ad custodiam ignis,: parvo nepoti,: vallo,.—
Fig., to bestow care or attention upon a thing, to watch, to watch for.
Absol.: exquire, heus tu, advigila,: tanto magis te advigilare aequomst,: si advigilaveris,.—
With pro: si advigilamus pro rei dignitate, Q. Cic. Petr. Cons. fin.—
With dat.: stupris,: sibi,.

la:noun:advocatio.html:
advŏcātĭo, ōnis, f.
advoco
,
a calling to or summoning (in the class. per. only as t. t. in judicial lang.).
Lit., abstr., legal assistance, judicial aid (v. advoco and advocatus): tu in re militari multo es cautior quam in advocationibus,.—
Transf.
Concr., legal assistance, the whole body of assistants, counsel (= the bar): haec advocatio,: so ; ; ; ; ; ; —
The time allowed for procuring legal assistance: ut binas advocationes postulent, Manut.; .—Hence,
Any kind of delay or adjournment (freq. in Seneca): ratio advocationem sibi petit, ira festinat, Sen. de Ira, 1, 16; so ; .—
Consolation, ; v. advoco, II. C.
